title: The recovery methods workshop
subtitle: Choose a method by the mixture and the substance you need
objective: Choose and justify filtration, evaporation or evaporation with condensation for a stated recovery target.

sow.exactOutcome: Investigate recovering substances from reversible changes.
sow.alignment: Intentional improved revisit: historical GROW Solubility_And_Recovery/Gettting_The_Solid_Back lessons cover related content. Original secondary-age exemplar at an upper-KS2 conceptual level; no qualification approval or completion claim.

priorLearning: Know that a solution contains a dissolved substance and a solvent.
success: Identify the mixture and desired recovered substance.
Explain what passes through a filter and what remains.
Sequence a recovery route and account for each component.

vocabulary.meaning: Separating an insoluble solid from a fluid using a filter.
Fluid that passes through a filter.
Liquid changing to gas at its surface.
The substance or substances that a method is intended to collect.

equipment: Shared mixture/target cards, selected route, pencils; optional sequencing tokens.
preparation: Default lesson is a process simulation and paper investigation. No heated separation apparatus is used.
Name the target before choosing a method. The model follows sand, salt and water; it does not certify drinking-water purity.
safety: Do not heat, boil, distil or taste any classroom mixture as part of this pack.
The evaporation/condensation diagram is a schematic of processes, not an apparatus construction guide.
Optional physical filtration would require a separately prepared school method; all necessary evidence is already supplied.
practicalAlternative: Use the four recovery briefs and process cards. Screen process choices and paper sequencing both provide the complete investigation.

misconceptions.claim: A filter removes dissolved salt from water.
misconceptions.correction: Dissolved salt passes with water through ordinary filter paper; sand can be retained.
misconceptions.check: Ask where the salt appears after filtering.

misconceptions.claim: Evaporation automatically gives collected liquid water.
misconceptions.correction: Open evaporation lets water vapour escape; collecting water requires capture and condensation.
misconceptions.check: Ask where the target water ends up.

misconceptions.claim: One separation method works for every mixture and target.
misconceptions.correction: The method depends on component properties and what you want to collect.
misconceptions.check: Compare saltwater target salt with saltwater target water.

access.supported: Match mixture/target pairs to process cards.
access.standard: Explain four routes and account for components.
access.stretch: Evaluate multistep recovery, loss and limits of purity claims.
access.regulation: Offer private writing, pointing, drawing or adult scribing. Allow pass-and-return for public questions and desk-based participation. Choose support from current learning evidence, not fixed ability labels.

slides.title: Same mixture, different mission
body: Two teams receive saltwater.
One wants salt; one wants water.
Should their methods be identical?
slides.notes: Start with target choice. The learner controls a process model, not real heating equipment.

slides.title: Recover the mixture ideas
body: R1. Is dissolved salt still present?
R2. What does evaporation change?
R3. What is condensation?
slides.notes: Yes. Evaporation changes liquid to gas at a surface; condensation changes gas to liquid. Evaporation can occur below the boiling temperature.

slides.title: I decide what the filter can retain
body: Sand remains as residue.
Salt and water pass as filtrate.
Clear filtrate is not proof of pure water.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I look at solubility, not just appearance. The ordinary filter catches sand grains but does not remove dissolved salt. The diagram is schematic; blue liquid below still contains salt.

visual.title: Filtration of sand mixed with saltwater
visual.description: A schematic funnel and filter paper retain sand above the filter. Salt solution passes through and is collected below. Labels distinguish sand residue and filtrate still containing dissolved salt. Purple symbols represent dissolved salt; the larger brown grains represent retained sand.

elements.text: A filter retains sand, not dissolved salt

Purple symbols: dissolved salt.
Schematic only; particles and pores are not to scale.

slides.title: I target the dissolved solid
body: Removing water can leave salt behind.
Open evaporation loses water into the air.
This suits a salt target, not a collected-water target.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Model the target statement first: I need salt. Then trace the water leaving and salt remaining. No heating is requested; evaporation can occur over time at room temperature.

visual.title: Evaporation leaves dissolved salt behind
visual.description: A process model shows salt solution at left and salt remaining in a dish at right after water has evaporated into surrounding air. Water is not collected by this open process.

elements.text:
Water vapour
leaves into the air
Open evaporation does not collect the water.

slides.title: I change the plan when the target changes
body: To collect water, capture its vapour.
Cool the vapour so it condenses.
The collected liquid is the target.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. The combined processes are the basis of distillation; naming distillation is optional. This is not a build diagram and does not certify drinking-water safety.

visual.title: Target: recover water from saltwater
visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Salt solution; Water evaporates;
salt remains; Vapour cools
and condenses. Capture the vapour and collect the liquid water.
Process schematic only; not an apparatus-building guide.

elements.text:
Capture the vapour and collect the liquid water.
Process schematic only; not an apparatus-building guide.

slides.title: Recovery workshop: choose, run, explain
body: W1. Choose methods for briefs A, B and C.
Name the recovered substance each time.
Test the process model or use paper arrows.
slides.notes: A: filter to collect sand. B: evaporate water to leave salt. C: capture water vapour and condense it to collect water. Ask pupils to account for both components.

slides.title: Two targets need a sequence
body: W2. Plan brief D.
What must happen before salt recovery?
Identify residue and filtrate.
slides.notes: Filter first: sand remains as residue and saltwater passes through as filtrate. Evaporate water from the filtrate to collect salt. Sand may need washing and drying for cleaner recovery; added wash water must be included when accounting for the mixture.

slides.title: Repair the purity claim
body: W3. “The liquid passed a filter, so it is safe to drink.”
Use the dissolved-salt evidence to challenge it.
slides.notes: Ordinary filtration does not reliably remove dissolved substances or microbes. Do not drink the mixtures. A clear liquid is not proven pure or safe.
slides.reveal: Ordinary filtration can leave dissolved substances in the liquid. Appearance does not prove purity or safety.

slides.title: A team wants water from saltwater
body: Which process plan matches that target?
slides.notes: A chooses the wrong target. B correctly captures and condenses water vapour. C fails because ordinary filtration does not remove dissolved salt.

options.text: Let water evaporate into the room and keep the salt.
options.feedback: That recovers salt while losing the target water.

options.text: Capture water vapour and condense it into a collecting container.
options.feedback: The target water is collected again as liquid.

options.text: Filter once and assume all dissolved salt is trapped.
options.feedback: Dissolved salt passes through ordinary filter paper.

slides.title: Your independent investigation
body: Choose one response route.
Match each mixture to its recovery target.
Explain where each component ends up.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across the three You do slides. Supply shared page 1 and one selected route page. All routes target the stated science objective; a labelled drawing or independent dictated explanation is valid.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Name residue and filtrate when filtering.
Keep evaporation separate from collected condensation.
For more than one target, sequence the steps.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask pupils which evidence supports their explanation. Read prompts or scribe without supplying the scientific conclusion.

slides.title: Check before sharing
body: Does my explanation answer the question?
Have I named the evidence or process?
Have I kept the conclusion within its limits?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Use the route-specific worked answers to identify one precise next step.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Trace one chosen route aloud or on paper.
Ask where the other component goes.
Improve a recovery or purity claim.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Offer partner or private teacher feedback. Ask for one specific revision linked to evidence; no public ranking.

slides.title: A question worth investigating
body: Suggest one next question about this lesson’s evidence.
Choose a question whose answer would improve our model.
slides.notes: Lundy cycle: invite written, spoken or pointed suggestions. Select one feasible question and explain how the pupil contribution changes the next example or investigation.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: E1. What does ordinary filtration remove here?
E2. How can salt be recovered from saltwater?
E3. What extra process collects the water?
slides.notes: Insoluble sand is caught by the filter. Removing water by evaporation leaves salt. Capture vapour and condense it to collect water. E4 asks why clear filtered liquid is not necessarily pure or safe.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: recovery briefs
pupilPages.intro: All activities are process models and paper investigations. No heating, tasting or apparatus building is needed.

cards.title: A • Sand + water
cards.text: Target: collect the sand. Sand is insoluble in water and its grains can be trapped by ordinary filter paper.

cards.title: B • Salt + water
cards.text: Target: collect the dissolved salt. Salt solution passes through ordinary filter paper. Removing water can leave salt behind.

cards.title: C • Salt + water
cards.text: Target: collect the water. Letting it escape into room air does not collect it. Capture its vapour and cool it to liquid.

cards.title: D • Sand + salt + water
cards.text: Target: collect sand and salt separately. Sand is insoluble; salt is dissolved. Different components need a sequence of processes.

cards.title: Process choices
cards.text: Filter: retain insoluble solid. Evaporate: leave dissolved solid. Capture vapour and condense: collect solvent as liquid. Methods are models, not instructions to improvise heating.

cards.title: Limits
cards.text: No tasting or drinking. A method’s name does not prove complete recovery or safe drinking water; other contaminants and losses may be present.

blocks.prompt: W1. Choose a method for A–C and name each recovered target.
W2. Sequence D and label residue/filtrate.
W3. Explain why a clear filtrate is not proof of safe drinking water.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: choose the target
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Word bank: filter / evaporate / condense.

blocks.prompt: S1. Sand + water; target sand. Choose …
S2. Saltwater; target salt. Choose …
S3. Saltwater; target water. Choose …
choices: Let water escape into the room

blocks.prompt: S4. After filtering sand + saltwater, what stays on the filter and what passes through?
S5. Put D in order: evaporate the filtrate / filter out sand. Explain the first step.
S6. Does clear liquid mean safe drinking water?

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: workshop report
pupilPages.intro: Explain methods, not just their names.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the table for all four briefs.
N2. Explain why ordinary filtration does not recover dissolved salt.
N3. Explain why open evaporation does not collect water.
N4. In D, identify residue and filtrate after step 1 and explain step 2.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: account for every component
pupilPages.intro: Keep target, method and limitations clear.

blocks.prompt: T1. Compare two plans for saltwater: target salt versus target water. Track both components in each.
T2. Plan recovery of sand and salt separately from D. Explain why reversing the order is less useful for separation.
T3. A team recovers 4 g from a constructed starting 5 g of salt. Does the missing gram prove salt was destroyed? Give two plausible process limits.
T4. Evaluate “clear filtrate is pure and safe”. State what the method actually establishes and what remains uncertain.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: State the target in each answer.

blocks.prompt: E1. What does ordinary filtration remove in these cases?
E2. How can salt be recovered from saltwater?
E3. What must be added to evaporation if water is the recovery target?
E4. Why does clear appearance not prove purity or safety?
Reflection. Which recovery target changes the plan most?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: Dissolved salt remains present. Evaporation changes liquid to gas at its surface; it can occur below boiling. Condensation changes gas to liquid.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: A filtration gives sand residue; B evaporation leaves salt; C capture vapour and condense to collect water. D filter first, then evaporate saltwater filtrate; sand stays as residue. W3 dissolved substances may pass through and other contaminants may remain; clarity is not purity or drinking-water safety.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A loses the water target. B correct. C ordinary filtration does not trap dissolved salt.

answers.label: S1–S6
answers.answer: Filter; evaporate water; capture and condense; sand residue remains while saltwater passes; filter then evaporate filtrate; no, clarity alone is insufficient.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: A filter/sand; B evaporate/salt; C evaporate with capture and condensation/water; D filter then evaporate filtrate/sand and salt separately. N2 dissolved salt passes with the water through ordinary filter paper. N3 vapour escapes unless captured. N4 sand residue and saltwater filtrate; remove water from filtrate to leave salt.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 salt target: water leaves and salt remains; water target: capture and condense water vapour while salt remains at source. T2 filter sand before removing water from dissolved salt; evaporating first leaves mixed sand and salt rather than separate products. T3 sample may remain dissolved in unrecovered liquid, stick to apparatus/filter, spill, or be affected by measurement uncertainty. Missing measured mass is not proof of destruction. T4 filtration establishes separation of suitable insoluble particles, not all dissolved substances or microbes; no safety claim is justified.

answers.label: E1–E4 / assessment
answers.answer: Insoluble sand; remove water by evaporation; capture and condense vapour; dissolved contaminants can remain and appearance is insufficient. Secure: target-dependent route and component accounting. Re-teach method matching by asking where the desired component finishes. Reflection accepts a reasoned target comparison.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.
This is an improved application of earlier solubility and recovery work. The new focus is target-dependent selection, component accounting and a multistep mixture.
The interactive separation model uses exactly briefs A–D on paper. It animates a process sequence, not a complete apparatus or practical safety procedure.
Evaporation is not synonymous with boiling. Recovering water uses captured vapour and condensation; no distillation apparatus is built in this lesson.

interactive.title: Recovery workshop: predict the collected product
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
